notes.heading: Periods, groups and blocks
points: The periodic table is organised into periods (rows), groups (columns) and blocks.
The four blocks are s, p, d and f, named after the sublevel being filled.
A copy of the periodic table is in the data booklet.

notes.heading: Period number and valence electrons
points: Period number equals the outermost energy level occupied by electrons.
Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons.
Groups are numbered 1 to 18.
Know the names: group 1 alkali metals, group 17 halogens, transition elements, noble gases.

notes.heading: Periodicity and trends in properties
points: Periodicity means properties change in a pattern across a period and down a group.
Across a period, nuclear charge rises while shielding stays nearly constant, so atoms get smaller and hold electrons more tightly.
First ionization energy rises across a period; it falls down a group as energy levels and shielding increase.
Electronegativity rises across a period and falls down a group; atomic radius shows the reverse pattern.
Cations are smaller than their atoms; anions are larger. Ionic radius increases down a group.

notes.heading: Group trends: alkali metals and halogens
points: Down group 1, ionization energy falls and metallic character rises, so reactivity with water increases.
Alkali metal plus water gives hydrogen and the aqueous hydroxide: M(s) + H2O(l) → ½H2(g) + MOH(aq).
Down group 17, electronegativity and non-metallic character fall, so halogens become less reactive.
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide, e.g. ½F2 + Cl⁻ → F⁻ + ½Cl2; the reverse does not occur.

notes.heading: Metal and non-metal oxides; acid deposition
points: Metallic and non-metallic character form a continuum; across a period oxides go from basic to amphoteric to acidic.
Period 3 oxides: Na2O and MgO basic, Al2O3 amphoteric, SiO2, P4O10, SO3 and SO2 acidic.
Metal oxides react with water to give hydroxides; non-metal oxides give acids, e.g. SO2 + H2O → H2SO3.
Amphoteric Al2O3 reacts with both acids and bases.
Rain is naturally about pH 5.6 from CO2; acid rain (below 5.6) comes from SO2 and nitrogen oxides. Dissolved CO2 acidifies oceans, harming corals and shellfish.

notes.heading: Oxidation states and rules
points: Oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if the compound were fully ionic; write it as +2 or –1.
Free element is 0; atoms in a neutral compound sum to 0; in a polyatomic ion they sum to the ion's charge.
Fluorine is –1; group 1 is +1; group 2 is +2; oxygen is –2 except in peroxides (–1) and OF2 (+2).
Hydrogen is +1 with non-metals and –1 in metal hydrides.
Oxyanions use Roman numerals, e.g. manganate(VII); nitrate(V) = nitrate, sulfate(IV) = sulfite are acceptable generic names.

notes.heading: Discontinuities in first ionization energy
points: Ionization energy dips from group 2 to 13 (Be to B) and from group 15 to 16 (N to O).
Be to B: boron's outer electron is in a higher-energy 2p sublevel, further out and shielded by 2s, so easier to remove.
N to O: oxygen's paired 2p electrons repel each other, so the removed electron needs less energy.
Explain using the energy of the electron removed, not special stability.

notes.heading: Properties of transition elements
points: A transition element has a partially filled d-sublevel, or forms a stable cation with an incomplete d-sublevel.
Strong attraction between delocalized d electrons and metal ions gives high melting points.
Many are good heterogeneous catalysts: reactants adsorb on the solid surface, react, and products desorb.
Zinc is d-block but not transition: Zn²⁺ keeps a full 3d10 sublevel.
Chromium is [Ar]4s¹3d⁵ and copper [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰ rather than the expected fillings.

notes.heading: Variable oxidation states
points: Transition elements form stable ions in several oxidation states.
This is because their successive ionization energies are close in value, so losing further electrons costs little extra.
Chromium has very small increases between successive ionization energies, so +1 to +6 are possible.
Copper has larger jumps, so only Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺ are common.
Common oxidation states of transition elements are in the data booklet.

notes.heading: Colour of transition element complexes
points: Ligands donate lone pairs to the central cation, forming coordination bonds in a complex ion.
Ligands split the five degenerate d orbitals into two sets of different energy.
An electron is promoted between split d orbitals when light matching the energy gap is absorbed.
Observed colour is the complementary colour of the light absorbed (opposite on the colour wheel).
Use c = λf and E = hf (h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s); wavelength in metres. Larger splitting means shorter wavelength absorbed.
Ion charge, ligand identity and metal identity all change the splitting and therefore the colour.

definitions.definition: The repeating trends in properties of elements across a period and down a group of the periodic table.
The minimum energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms in the ground state.
definitions.trap: Leaving out the word gaseous, which most candidates missed.

definitions.definition: The ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons in a covalent bond to itself.
definitions.trap: Saying it attracts a single electron, or omitting the bonding pair.

definitions.definition: The energy released when an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom, forming a 1– ion.
The reduced attraction a valence electron feels from the nucleus because inner electrons shield part of the positive charge.
Atoms or ions that have the same electron configuration, though different numbers of protons.
definitions.trap: Thinking same electron configuration means same size; more protons means a smaller radius.

definitions.definition: A substance that can act as both an acid and a base, reacting with both acids and bases.
The charge an atom would have if the compound were made entirely of ions, showing electrons transferred.
definitions.trap: Writing 2+ or 2 instead of +2; the sign comes first.

definitions.definition: An element with a partially filled d-sublevel, or one that forms a stable cation with an incomplete d-sublevel.
definitions.trap: Calling zinc a transition element; Zn²⁺ has a full d-sublevel.

definitions.definition: A molecule or ion with a lone pair of electrons that it donates to a central metal cation, forming a coordination bond.
definitions.trap: Poorly defined even by strong candidates; always mention the donated lone pair.

definitions.definition: A central transition element cation bonded to ligands by coordination bonds.
Orbitals of the same energy, such as the five d orbitals in an isolated ion.
A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, which lowers activation energy and is not used up.
